newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: WHO confirms cholera outbreak in eastern Zaire.
newsitem.headline: WHO confirms cholera outbreak in eastern Zaire.

text.p: The World Health Organisation said on Friday that cases of cholera had been confirmed in eastern Zaire and it feared further outbreaks in the strife-torn area.
Laboratory tests on samples taken from 14 Zairean patients, who arrived in Goma's central hospital from the town of Sake, have confirmed cholera, according to the U.N. agency.
Sake is 30 km (18 miles) to the west of Goma, in the middle of an area of fighting cut off from foreign aid and clogged with refugees.

"All the elements are there for a dramatic situation -- cholera and possibly other epidemics combined with malnutrition and war wounds," said Dr Maria Neira, who coordinates the WHO's global task force on cholera.
"We have confirmed cases from Sake, but there could very well be cases around Bukavu and a little bit all over the place," the Spanish doctor told Reuters.

A medical charity said earlier this week that an Argentine doctor was battling alone to treat cholera sufferers among a mass of Rwandan Hutu refugees camped around the hillside town of Mwenga, 80 km (50 miles) southwest of Bukavu.

Medicos en Catastrofe Internacional (Doctors in International Catastrophes) said Dr Abel Pasqualini estimated there were 250,000 refugees at the site. He was the only doctor who had reached the makeshift camp.
Neira, who is heading to Kigali on Sunday, appealed for access to the area so medical aid could get through.
"We don't know what is happening in Sake. We appeal to be able to reach these people and give them medical assistance," she said.

The U.N. Security Council is preparing to vote on a resolution to send a multinational force to ease the plight of an estimated 1.2 million Hutu refugees from Rwanda and Burundi scattered across eastern Zaire.
About 30,000 people are believed to have died in 1994 from cholera in Africa's Great Lakes region when Rwandan Hutus fled after Hutu-led genocide of minority Tutsis.
Neira was asked whether she feared a cholera outbreak on the same scale. "I won't speculate but it is a very dangerous situation," she replied.
She and Dr Fabrizio Bassini, an Italian who directs WHO's emergency operations, are part of the three-strong WHO team flying to Zaire over the weekend.
Neira told a news briefing the Geneva-based agency fears outbreaks of other diseases, including a form of bloody diarrhoea known as shigellosis which has an even higher mortality rate than cholera.

The condition of the 14 patients in Goma was not known at present but they were believed to have survived, Neira said. Most were in stable condition when a WHO epidemiologist left the town earlier this week.
